name: Bone age X-ray (growth plate check)

card.summary: A hand and wrist X-ray used by pediatric clinicians to gauge skeletal maturity, and by height-focused forum users to ask whether growth plates are still open.
card.aka: Bone age scan; skeletal age assessment; growth plate X-ray; Greulich-Pyle
card.note: A validated clinical test in children; as an adult 'growth potential' check it is an informal use, and results are approximate.

quick.overview:
A bone age X-ray images the left hand and wrist and compares the bones with reference standards to estimate how mature the skeleton is. Clinicians use it to evaluate growth disorders, early or delayed puberty, and to estimate remaining growth in children.

In looksmaxxing communities, people post their results and ask whether their growth plates are open or closed, often with the aim of knowing whether height gain is still possible. Online threads also debate whether anabolic steroids, growth hormone or peptides advance bone age.
quick.mechanism: Growth plates are cartilage zones near the ends of long bones where lengthening happens; rising sex hormones, especially estrogen, drive their maturation and eventual replacement by bone. The X-ray reads the appearance of the wrist and hand bones against an atlas (Greulich-Pyle) or scores individual bones (Tanner-Whitehouse). Software and deep-learning tools have also been developed.
quick.risks: The radiation dose from a hand X-ray is described as low. Results are estimates with inter-observer variability, and the commonly used atlas was built from mid-twentieth-century US children, so accuracy may differ for other populations. A bone age reading alone does not predict a specific adult height.

lead: Bone age is the degree of skeletal maturity, usually assessed from a radiograph of the left hand and wrist and expressed as the age at which an average child shows the same development [1][2]. For anyone trying to look taller, it answers a concrete question: how much of the skeleton's growth is already behind it, and whether the growth plates that lengthen the legs and spine are still active. A reading near or beyond adult maturity tells a person that height-focused plans such as growth-oriented treatments are unlikely to add length, while an immature reading tells a younger person that growth is still ongoing, which can inform decisions about nutrition, sleep, medical review and expectations [1][7].

Clinicians use bone age to help diagnose and monitor conditions such as constitutional growth delay, precocious puberty, thyroid disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia and growth hormone deficiency, and to predict adult height [1][2]. A bone age that differs from chronological age by more than two standard deviations is generally regarded as abnormal [1]. The two best-known methods are the Greulich and Pyle atlas, first published in 1950, in which a reader matches the radiograph to reference images, and the Tanner-Whitehouse method, in which individual bones are graded and summed [1][2]. Computer-based systems, including deep-learning models evaluated in the RSNA Pediatric Bone Age Machine Learning Challenge, have been developed to reduce subjectivity [3][4].

In looksmaxxing and height forums, a bone age or growth plate X-ray is treated as the way to find out whether further height growth is biologically possible. Users post their reports and images, compare results with their chronological age, and debate how substances such as anabolic steroids, growth hormone or peptides might influence skeletal maturation [5][6].

angle.text: The scan does not add height itself. It tells a person how mature the skeleton is, which for teenagers and young adults indicates whether any growth remains. People use the result to set height expectations and to decide whether growth-related plans make sense, or whether to focus on posture, grooming, build and other appearance factors.

paras: Long bones grow in length at growth plates (epiphyseal plates), plates of hyaline cartilage near each end of the bone. Cells in the plate divide, stack, enlarge and then die, and the calcified matrix they leave behind is converted into bone, which pushes the ends of the bone apart. The plate is organised in five zones: reserve, proliferation (stimulated by growth hormone), maturation and hypertrophy, calcification, and ossification [7]. In adults the plate has been replaced by a bony epiphyseal line [7].

Wikipedia states that complete fusion can occur as early as age 12 in girls and 14 in boys, most commonly at 14 to 15 and 15 to 17 respectively [7]. Bone maturity in general is reached at roughly 15 to 17 in boys and 14 to 16 in girls, and peak height velocity occurs on average around age 11 in girls and 13 in boys [1]. Females therefore stop growing about two years earlier than males on average [1].

Rising estrogen during puberty, in both males and females, increases chondrocyte cell death in the growth plate, slowing and eventually ending growth [7]. A 1995 case report of siblings with aromatase deficiency, a condition in which the body cannot make estrogen from androgens, is widely cited in the endocrine literature as evidence of estrogen's role in skeletal maturation in both sexes [8]. Wikipedia's testosterone article likewise says bone maturation is completed indirectly through estradiol metabolites [11].

The left hand and wrist are used because they are easy to image with little radiation and display many small bones in a single view; the left side is used because most people are right-hand dominant and the non-dominant hand is less likely to have been deformed by injury [1]. The first carpal ossification center, the capitate, appears around 2 months of age, followed by the hamate and the triquetrum at about 14 months, and the pattern of centers, bone shapes and epiphyseal fusion then changes in a predictable order through childhood and adolescence [1].

In a late-teen or adult report, the radiologist describes whether the epiphyses of the radius, ulna and hand bones are open, partly fused or fully fused. Delayed bone age can accompany growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism and constitutional delay of growth, while advanced bone age can accompany precocious puberty, congenital adrenal hyperplasia and obesity [1].

The first atlas of the left hand and wrist was published by John Poland in 1898; Greulich and Pyle published their atlas in 1950, and Tanner and Whitehouse published their scoring method in 1962, with revisions in 1975 (TW2) and 2001 (TW3) [1]. Wikipedia credits William Walter Greulich and Sarah Idell Pyle with the atlas that remains the most common method in the United States, covering males from 3 months to 19 years and females from 3 months to 18 years [1]. Grokipedia credits T. Wingate Todd's radiographic collection as a basis of the Greulich-Pyle approach [2].

The Tanner-Whitehouse system is a single-bone method: TW3 scores the distal radius and ulna, the first, third and fifth metacarpals and phalanges, and all carpals except the pisiform [1]. Other approaches include a knee atlas by Pyle and Hoerr (1969), foot and ankle (1962) and elbow (1981) systems, cervical vertebra staging (Lamparski, 1972; Hassel and Farman, 1995), and MRI of the hand and wrist (Tomei, 2013) [1].

Wikipedia notes that the Greulich-Pyle atlas drew on healthy white children in the Brush Foundation study (1931 to 1942) in Cleveland, Ohio, and has not been updated since 1959, so it may be less accurate for other groups; different readers can assign different bone ages to the same radiograph [1].

Tables relate bone age to the percentage of adult height already attained, allowing a predicted adult height; the Bayley-Pinneau tables are included with the Greulich-Pyle atlas [1][2]. Wikipedia states that predictions are less accurate in atypical growth such as children born small for gestational age who remain short [1].

Recent studies have paired automated bone age readers with height prediction. Titles in the literature include a 2023 paper on deep-learning estimation of bone age and final adult height in the Yonsei Medical Journal and a 2025 comparison of bone-age-based and body-composition-based height prediction in Korean children [12][13]. These are pediatric studies; they address children who are still growing rather than adults asking whether growth has ended.

A 2018 study in Radiology reported performance of a deep-learning neural network in assessing skeletal maturity on pediatric hand radiographs [3], and the 2019 RSNA challenge compared machine-learning approaches on a large shared dataset [4]. Registered clinical studies have evaluated AI-based bone age software in Chinese children and in a validation study of 1,903 participants [9][10]. Developers describe such tools as a way to reduce inter- and intra-observer variability [1].

The method uses ionising radiation; imaging only the left hand and wrist is described as keeping exposure low, and cervical-vertebra methods can avoid an extra X-ray when a neck image already exists [1]. Ultrasound and MRI approaches are described as non-ionising alternatives that require further validation [2], and radiation-free ultrasound models for estimating bone age continue to appear in the radiology literature [14]. A 2024 phantom study examined a self-shielded bone age X-ray instrument against scattered radiation in children [15].

Estrogen and androgens are central to the timing of plate closure. Wikipedia's page on anabolic-androgenic steroids lists premature epiphyseal closure and short stature among adverse effects described in children, and describes androgens as speeding bone maturation in adolescents, partly through estrogen metabolites; the page tags the claim about reduced adult height at high doses as needing a citation [16]. It also notes that low-dose oxandrolone has been used for idiopathic short stature but may accelerate maturation without increasing final height [16]. An older report in JAMA (1965) concerned growth and bone-age retardation in cystic fibrosis and the response to an anabolic steroid, illustrating that bone age has long been used to monitor such treatments [17].

The strength training article notes that earlier concerns about lifting and growth plates were tied to poor supervision, bad form or excessive loads, and that the National Strength and Conditioning Association states properly designed, supervised training is safe for children [18].

Height-focused communities treat the growth plate scan as a decisive checkpoint. Threads titled around getting a growth plate X-ray the next day, or a long-awaited result, are common [19][20]. In one looksmax.org thread, a 16-year-10-month-old user reported that his scan gave an estimated bone age of 17 and an "appropriate bone age", and that he took this to mean his plates were closing or closed; he wrote that he had hoped for room to grow with growth hormone, and that he would now focus on other looksmaxxing areas [19].

Users also discuss whether androgens, growth hormone or peptides could advance or preserve bone age, and ask clinicians and each other for interpretations of reports. Some propose theories involving senolytic compounds or peptides to slow maturation; these are community hypotheses rather than studied interventions [5][6].

Human research on bone age assessment is extensive in pediatric endocrinology, including the deep-learning and machine-learning validation studies above [3][4][9][10], and studies of adult height prediction using automated bone age [12][13]. No studies found test whether the substances discussed in forum threads slow bone age advancement in healthy people.

lore.intro: On height-focused forums, bone age and growth plate X-rays are discussed as the arbiter of whether further height gain is possible, and as a way to test ideas about how hormones and peptides affect skeletal maturation.

claims.claim: A wrist X-ray shows whether you can still grow taller.
claims.believers: Users post radiographs and ask for readings of open or closed plates, treating the result as decisive for height plans [19][20].
claims.experts: Clinicians use bone age with current height and tables to estimate remaining growth in children, with variability between readers and less accuracy in atypical growth [1]. Adult height is generally considered to end once plates fuse [7].

claims.claim: A bone age at or above your actual age means you are done growing.
claims.believers: A forum user whose report gave a bone age of 17 at age 16 years 10 months read it as plates closing or closed [19].
claims.experts: Radiology reports describe such a result as an appropriate bone age; plate fusion typically occurs at 15 to 17 in males, with individual variation [1][7]. Reports describe an estimate, and readers can differ [1].

claims.claim: Anabolic steroids, growth hormone and peptides can accelerate bone age and fuse the plates early.
claims.believers: Forum users planned scans after heavy use of androgens and growth hormone to test whether bone age had advanced beyond chronological age [5].
claims.experts: Estrogen, including estrogen made from androgens, is described as driving growth plate maturation [7][8][11]. Reference sources describe premature epiphyseal closure as an adverse effect of anabolic steroids in children [16]. No published study tests this for the specific substances and patterns described in the threads.

claims.claim: Lifting heavy before the plates close stunts growth.
claims.believers: A long-running looksmax.org thread argued that heavy lifting in the early teens ends in shorter adults, though replies in the same thread disputed it [21].
claims.experts: The strength training article reports that the NSCA considers properly supervised training safe for children and attributes earlier concern to poor technique or excessive loads [18].

claims.claim: A stack of a senolytic, a bioregulator peptide and a PTH analogue could keep bone age younger.
claims.believers: The thread's author describes a theory that clearing senescent cells in growth cartilage might slow maturation [6].
claims.experts: No published human studies were found testing this combination for slowing bone age.

claims.claim: Bone age tables tell you your exact adult height.
claims.believers: Some users treat a predicted adult height from a bone age report as a firm number.
claims.experts: Tables such as Bayley-Pinneau give predictions that are less accurate in atypical growth, and the Greulich-Pyle reference population was a narrow group of mid-century children [1]. Automated height predictors are being studied in pediatric cohorts [12][13].
